name: wire-tap
intent: Interpose a fixed recipient list on a channel that publishes every message unmodified to the primary receiver and to a secondary channel, so tests, monitors and troubleshooting tools can inspect live traffic without changing the primary flow.
problem: Operators need to inspect the messages actually travelling over a point-to-point channel, but adding capture code to the sender or the receiver mixes observation into application components, changes the component under test and risks altering the very behaviour that is being observed.
context: Live message channels, typically point-to-point document messages, where the traffic must keep flowing untouched, the observing component is separate from both sender and receiver, and the secondary copy may be sampled, lagging or lossy; also used when a realistic message sample is needed for testing, monitoring or troubleshooting.
benefits: Observation is non-invasive: the primary receiver still gets every message, unmodified, and neither sender nor receiver code changes.
A single generic tap can be inserted into any channel, so the instrumentation logic is written once and reused instead of being rebuilt per component.
Analysis logic lives in a second component: inspectors can be added, replaced or stopped without touching the application flow.
Enables production-traffic use cases that are otherwise hard to obtain: monitoring, auditing, anomaly detection and replaying realistic payloads into tests.
Instrumentation becomes a reversible configuration change: a tap can be enabled for a diagnosis window and removed afterwards, which lowers the risk of touching a working solution.
Observation cadence is decoupled from processing cadence: within its buffer the tap consumer may be slower than the flow without stalling it.
tradeoffs: Every message is duplicated, so the tap costs bandwidth, storage and CPU in proportion to traffic even when nobody reads the secondary channel.

Asynchronous taps are lossy by construction: bounded queues drop or overwrite copies when the analyzer lags (Camel falls back to a synchronous send when its executor pool is exhausted, ZeroMQ capture drops for slow subscribers, tokio broadcast overwrites and reports lag), so the copy is evidence, not a guarantee.

A synchronous tap reverses the dependency: the analysis component's latency and outages become the primary flow's, so tap failures are usually swallowed instead - and a silently dead tap removes observability exactly when it is needed.
The secondary copy is a second place where sensitive payloads live; it needs its own redaction, access control and retention rules.

Channel-level copying is not always a deep copy: analyzers that receive the live object can mutate or block the message the primary path still uses unless the tap explicitly serializes or prepares an independent copy.
Tap placement and count matter: copies show pre- or post-translation payloads depending on where the tap sits, and each additional tap multiplies the duplicated traffic.

participants.responsibility: Fixed recipient list with two outputs: consumes messages from the input side, publishes each message unmodified to the primary output and a copy to the secondary channel, and never blocks the primary path.
The original destination that keeps receiving every message, unchanged and unimpeded, exactly as before the tap was inserted.
The additional channel that carries the copies to the analysis component; its capacity, loss policy and lifecycle belong to the tap, not to the flow.
Separate component (logger, monitor, audit store, test harness) that inspects the copied messages and can be changed or stopped without affecting the primary flow.

use_cases: Capture production traffic into a log or store to diagnose a defect that cannot be reproduced in staging.
Feed monitoring, audit and anomaly detection from a live channel without redeploying or touching the applications.
Mirror a sample of real messages into a test harness so tests replay realistic payloads instead of hand-written fixtures.
Validate a new message translator, mapper or canonical data model against real traffic before cutover.
Build a shadow record of what a legacy consumer receives, as input to message history or message store analysis.
Feed a security or data-loss-prevention scanner with copies of messages while the business flow continues.

Shadow-test a new service version against live traffic with Istio/Envoy request mirroring (VirtualService mirror + mirrorPercentage, or the Gateway API RequestMirror filter): Envoy copies each request out of band with -shadow appended to the Host/Authority header and discards the mirrored response, so only the primary response reaches users.

Mirror topic streams continuously to another Kafka cluster with Apache Kafka MirrorMaker 2 - data with partition order preserved, plus topic config, ACLs and consumer-group offsets emitted as checkpoint topics with heartbeat topics proving the mirror is alive; this is the durable end of the wire-tap spectrum, replayable for disaster recovery and consumer migration rather than a best-effort diagnostic copy.
avoid_when: The inspecting component already receives the message itself: log or handle it there instead of adding a tap.
A one-off look at the traffic is enough: a broker trace facility, a test message or a debugger is simpler than a production tap.
Copies must be complete, ordered and durable: use a message store or broker-native audit/tracing, because a wire tap is deliberately best-effort and lossy.
The channel is already publish-subscribe and the analyzer can simply be one more subscriber: subscribe instead of re-routing messages.
The tap would duplicate traffic that is already large: sample at the source or use aggregated metrics instead of copying every payload.

The tapped flow's handlers have externally visible side effects: the copy is a real message, so running the same consumer against a shadow target duplicates writes, emails and payments - point the secondary channel only at side-effect-free analyzers or a sandboxed cluster.

The secondary consumer must respond to or take over the traffic: a wire tap's output is strictly receive-only; conditional routing with a bypass is a Detour, and letting several consumers share the primary queue is Competing Consumers, not a tap.
anti_patterns: The synchronously coupled tap: the analyzer is invoked in-band, so its outage or latency becomes a flow outage - that is a Detour or a filter, not a wire tap.
Mutating or enriching the message inside the tap so the primary receiver observes changed data (adding headers on a shared in-process object is the classic version of this bug).
Tapping with an unbounded secondary buffer and full payloads forever, turning a diagnostic aid into a memory leak and a data-protection liability.
Subscribing the analyzer to the point-to-point channel itself, which steals messages from the primary receiver instead of copying them.
Treating the best-effort tap copy as the audit of record, then discovering the gaps during the incident it was supposed to explain.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: forwarding messages and observing messages are different responsibilities, and the observer lives in its own component.
Open/closed principle: observability is added by re-wiring the channel, without modifying sender or receiver.
Information hiding and minimal coupling: the analysis component knows only the secondary channel, never the applications.
Fail-safe default: observation must not be able to break the observed flow, which forces an explicit loss policy instead of silent coupling.
Reuse: one generic tap works for any channel instead of instrumentation code per component.
best_practices: Copy before sharing: hand the analyzer an independent copy (serialized or deep-cloned), never the live message object.
Deliver out of band through a bounded queue and choose an explicit overflow policy (drop oldest, overwrite, sample); expose counters for drops and lag.
Publish the message unmodified: enrichment and transformation belong to the analyzer, not to the tap.
Scope the tap narrowly and document whether the copies are pre- or post-translation; at high volume, sample instead of copying everything.
Give the copy its own lifecycle: redact sensitive fields, expire it, and restrict access like any other copy of production data.
Make the tap controllable and watched: a runtime switch (control bus) plus a watchdog, so a silently dead tap is noticed.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Wire Tap (Systems Management chapter).
pitfalls: Assuming the tap deep-copies the payload: Camel's .wireTap copies only the Exchange while body and header objects stay shared with the original, so an analyzer that mutates a field changes what the primary path sees - deep-clone or serialize in onPrepare before the copy leaves the tap.

Invoking the analyzer in-band: Spring Integration's WireTap interceptor runs on the sender's thread unless the tap target is an executor/queue channel, and Camel sends tapped messages synchronously by the calling thread once its wire-tap thread pool is exhausted - a slow or down analyzer then injects its latency and outage into the primary flow; make the secondary leg explicitly asynchronous or give the tap its own executor.

Treating the tap copy as the audit of record: asynchronous taps drop copies by design (queue overflow, ZeroMQ slow-subscriber drops, tokio Lagged), so gaps appear exactly in the incident being reconstructed - use a message store, broker-native tracing, or durable mirroring (Kafka MirrorMaker 2) when completeness is required.

Consuming the point-to-point channel itself instead of the tap's own secondary channel: against a competing-consumers queue this steals messages from the primary receiver - an invisible load-balancer, not observation.

Never exporting drop counters or expiry rules: every overflow policy (DropOldest, select default branch, Lagged) is silent, so a tap that has been dead for weeks looks healthy, and retained full payloads become a data-protection liability - publish drop/lag metrics, alarm on them, and redact and expire the copies like any other production data.

related_patterns_notes.spy: A Spy records calls made to an in-process object so a test can later assert on its interactions, while a Wire Tap copies channel traffic out of process to an analyzer; if the observed thing is a method call inside the system under test, use a Spy.
related_patterns_notes.mock: A Mock preprograms responses and verifies interactions at an in-process test boundary, whereas a Wire Tap never responds and only observes real traffic; if the test needs the inspected component to influence behaviour, a tap is the wrong tool.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: An Interceptor wraps a single invocation in-process and may alter it, while a Wire Tap interposes out-of-band on the channel and must alter nothing by contract - Spring Integration indeed realizes the Wire Tap as a ChannelInterceptor.
related_patterns_notes.audit-interceptor: An Audit Interceptor emits structured, accountability-grade security events from the endpoint it protects, while a Wire Tap produces raw copies of channel traffic that an audit component may consume; they compose, with the tap feeding the audit pipeline.
related_patterns_notes.observer: Observer couples an in-process subject to listeners that may react and change shared state, while a Wire Tap is its messaging-scale counterpart: copies travel to independent analyzers on a separate channel with no feedback into the flow.
